###NOTE: only H2 was applicable for the correlation analysis.###
I completed the steps for H1 satisfaction_commitment composite, but the other variable (infidelity) is categorical, and thus correlation is not appropriate. Not sure if the composite variable still needs normalization in this case. 

## 1. Load the processed data

```{r load}
# Open the project's .Rproj file before running chunks.
# Install psych once in the Console if needed: install.packages("psych")
library(psych)

h1Data <- read.csv("script/data/processed_data/practice_h1.csv")
h2Data <- read.csv("script/data/processed_data/practice_h2.csv")

```

## 2. Look at the distribution first

```{r histogram}
# A histogram groups numerical values into intervals (bins).
# Bar height shows how many observations fall in each interval.
# Start by looking at the distribution before calculating summary statistics.
# Add readable labels to the same histogram.
hist(h1Data$satisfaction_commitment,
     main = "Distribution of relationship satisfaction & commitment",
     xlab = "Relationship satisfaction & commitment")

hist(h2Data$Age,
     main = "Distribution of age",
     xlab = "Age (18-90")

hist(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1,
     main = "Distribution of willingness to marry without love",
     xlab = "Willingness to marry without love")
```

## 3. One statistic at a time

```{r individual_statistics}
## H1 ##
#count:0 NA
sum(is.na(h1Data$satisfaction_commitment))

# Mean: add the scores and divide by the number of observed responses, no NAs to remove: 5.71
mean(h1Data$satisfaction_commitment, na.rm = F)
# Median: the middle score after sorting the responses: 6
median(h1Data$satisfaction_commitment, na.rm = F)

# Table: count how many people are in each category: 31269 no infidelity, 19050 infidelity
table(h1Data$infidelity, useNA = "ifany")

# Range: return the minimum and maximum, rather than their difference: 1-7 (composite of 1-7 Likert)
range(h1Data$satisfaction_commitment, na.rm = F)

# IQR: the 75th percentile minus the 25th percentile: 1.5
IQR(h1Data$satisfaction_commitment, na.rm = F)

## H2 ##
#count:0 NA for both
sum(is.na(h2Data$Age))
sum(is.na(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1))

# Mean: add the scores and divide by the number of observed responses, no NAs to remove
mean(h2Data$Age, na.rm = F) #30.24
mean(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1, na.rm = F) #38.46

# Median: the middle score after sorting the responses
median(h2Data$Age, na.rm = F) #25
median(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1, na.rm = F) #30

# Range: return the minimum and maximum, rather than their difference: 1-7 (composite of 1-7 Likert)
range(h2Data$Age, na.rm = F) #18-90
range(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1, na.rm = F) #0-100

# IQR: the 75th percentile minus the 25th percentile: 1.5
IQR(h2Data$Age, na.rm = F) #15
IQR(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1, na.rm = F) #65
```

## 4. Standardize a variable

```{r standardize}
# scale() uses z = (original score - mean) / standard deviation by default.
# Keep the original commitment scores and store the standardized values separately.
# scale() returns a matrix; as.numeric() makes a simple numeric column.

h1Data$satisfaction_commitment_z <- as.numeric(scale(h1Data$satisfaction_commitment))

h2Data$Age_z <- as.numeric(scale(h2Data$Age))

h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1_z <- as.numeric(scale(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1))

# Standardized scores have mean approximately 0 and standard deviation 1.
mean(h1Data$satisfaction_commitment_z, na.rm = T)
mean(h2Data$Age_z, na.rm = T)
mean(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1_z, na.rm = T)

sd(h1Data$satisfaction_commitment_z, na.rm = T)
sd(h2Data$Age_z, na.rm = T)
sd(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1_z, na.rm = T)

```

## 5. Covariance and correlation

```{r association}
# Covariance describes whether two variables tend to move together.
# Positive: higher values tend to occur together. Negative: higher values tend to accompany lower values.
# Its size depends on the units and is not restricted to -1 through 1.
#cov: -40.30
cov(h2Data$Age, h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1, use = "complete.obs") #only use when you have data for both

# Pearson correlation expresses a linear association on a -1 to 1 scale.
#cor: -0.096
cor(h2Data$Age, h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1, use = "complete.obs")

# Select numerical variables only; do not include participant IDs or category codes.
corDataH2 <- h2Data[, c("Age", "Love_would_you_marry_1")]

# A correlation matrix gives the correlation for each pair of columns.
# The diagonal is 1 because each variable is correlated with itself.
cor(corDataH2, use = "complete.obs")
```

## 6. Several statistics at once

```{r combined_summaries}
# summary() reports minimum, quartiles, median, mean, maximum, and missing counts when present.
summary(corDataH2)

# psych::describe() reports n, mean, SD, median, minimum, maximum, range width (max minus min), skewness, kurtosis, and other summaries.
# However it does not report every statistic above: compute IQR, cov(), and cor() separately.
psych::describe(corDataH2)
```
